missions.title: The Golden Lantern Adventure
missions.story: Maya investigates a missing festival lantern. Learners collect three clue cards by reading a continuing story and using evidence to solve the mystery.
missions.focus: Literary comprehension, story grammar, story sequencing, context clues, inference, prediction and summarizing.

finalChallenge.title: Restore the Festival
finalChallenge.description: Restore the Festival: arrange these seven story events in order: lantern missing; Maya volunteers; Lola Rosa mentions ribbon; Maya finds ribbon and footprints; Maya follows footprints; Librarian Nela explains; Maya returns lantern. Then choose or compose a 1–2 sentence summary.

steps.prompt: Restore the Festival: tap the seven story events in the order they happened.
items: The Golden Lantern is missing
Maya volunteers to find it
Lola Rosa mentions a red ribbon
Maya finds the ribbon and footprints
Maya follows the footprints
Librarian Nela explains what happened
Maya returns the lantern

steps.prompt: Now choose the best summary of the story.
items: Maya loves festivals and parades.
The Golden Lantern went missing, Maya followed clues to the library, and Librarian Nela had moved it to keep it safe, so Maya returned it.
Lola Rosa sells ribbons at the market near the garden.
Mayor Luis was angry about the festival.

checkpoints.title: Story Garden — The Missing Lantern
checkpoints.reading: On the morning of Brightville's festival, Mayor Luis discovered that the Golden Lantern was missing from its display at the town hall. The lantern was important because it would be carried during the opening parade. Maya, a curious and helpful learner, volunteered to find it.
checkpoints.lesson: A story has characters (who), a setting (where and when), and a problem (what needs to be solved). We can identify a character's traits from their actions.

miniGame.name: Story Detective
miniGame.instructions: Tap the character, place, and missing object shown on the scene; then match the labels Character, Setting and Problem.

steps.prompt: Story Detective: tap a card, then tap the label that matches it.
items: Maya
Mayor Luis
The town hall
The morning of Brightville's festival
The Golden Lantern is missing
steps.success: Great detective work! You found the character, setting and problem.

questions.text: Who is the main character in the story?
questions.feedback: Maya is the central character who volunteers to solve the problem.

questions.text: Where was the Golden Lantern displayed before it went missing?
questions.feedback: The story says the lantern was displayed at the town hall.

questions.text: What problem begins the story?
questions.feedback: Mayor Luis discovers that the Golden Lantern is missing.

questions.text: Which action best shows that Maya is helpful?
options: She visits the market for food
She volunteers to find the lantern
questions.feedback: Maya offers to help solve the town’s problem.

questions.text: Why is finding the lantern important to the town?
options: It will be used in the opening parade
It is a prize for a quiz
It lights the library every night
questions.feedback: The lantern is needed for the festival’s opening parade.

checkpoints.title: Truth Hall — Follow the Clues
checkpoints.reading: At the market, vendor Lola Rosa remembered seeing a red ribbon near the Story Garden. Maya searched the garden and found a red ribbon on a bench beside muddy footprints. She followed the footprints along a narrow path, just wide enough for one person, to the Word Library.
checkpoints.lesson: Sequence means putting events in the order they happened. Words like first, next, and finally help us understand order. Context clues in nearby words can explain an unfamiliar word. A prediction should use evidence from the story.

miniGame.name: Clue Path
miniGame.instructions: Arrange these five action cards: discover missing lantern → volunteer → ask vendor → find ribbon and footprints → follow footprints to library.

steps.prompt: Clue Path: tap the action cards in the order they happened.
items: Maya discovers the lantern is missing
Maya volunteers to find it
Maya asks the vendor
Maya finds the ribbon and footprints
Maya follows the footprints to the library
steps.success: You followed the clue path in the right order!

questions.text: Who told Maya about a red ribbon near the Story Garden?
questions.feedback: Lola Rosa remembered seeing the ribbon near the garden.

questions.text: What did Maya see beside the ribbon on the bench?
questions.feedback: The ribbon was beside muddy footprints, which gave Maya another clue.

questions.text: Which event happened immediately after Maya found the ribbon and footprints?
options: She followed the footprints to the library
questions.feedback: Maya followed the footprints along a path to the Word Library.

questions.text: The path was 'narrow, just wide enough for one person.' What does narrow mean?
questions.feedback: The phrase “just wide enough for one person” tells us the path was not wide.

questions.text: Before entering the library, what is Maya most likely to do next based on the footprints?
options: Look for more clues inside the library
questions.feedback: The footprints lead toward the library, so searching there is a reasonable prediction.

checkpoints.title: Word Library — Solve the Mystery
checkpoints.reading: Inside the Word Library, Librarian Nela explained that she had moved the lantern behind a tall bookcase to protect it from the storm the night before. She had forgotten to inform the mayor. Maya felt relieved and carried the lantern back to the town hall. Mayor Luis thanked her, and the festival began on time.
checkpoints.lesson: To infer, use clues in the story to understand feelings or meaning that may not be stated directly. A conclusion is an idea supported by evidence. A good summary includes the important problem, actions, and solution without adding unrelated details.

miniGame.name: Evidence Board
miniGame.instructions: Match these claims to evidence cards: Maya is helpful → volunteered / returned lantern; lantern was protected → Nela moved it before storm; mystery was solved → festival began on time.

steps.prompt: Evidence Board: which claim does each evidence card support?
items: Maya volunteered to find the lantern
Maya returned the lantern to the town hall
Librarian Nela moved the lantern before the storm
The festival began on time
steps.success: Every claim needs evidence, and you matched them well.

questions.text: Why did Librarian Nela move the Golden Lantern?
options: She wanted to keep it forever
She wanted to protect it from the storm
She wanted to cancel the festival
questions.feedback: Nela moved the lantern behind a bookcase for protection during the storm.

questions.text: How did Maya most likely feel when she learned where the lantern was?
questions.feedback: The story states Maya felt relieved because the lantern had been found.

questions.text: What conclusion is best supported by the story?
options: The lantern had been moved for safekeeping
Maya forgot the lantern at home
questions.feedback: Nela explains that she moved it to protect it from rain, not to steal it.

questions.text: Which is the best summary of the whole story?
options: Maya enjoys the festival and buys a ribbon
A storm destroys the village library
Lola Rosa asks Maya to become a librarian
Maya follows clues to find a lantern that was moved for safekeeping and returns it
questions.feedback: This choice includes the problem, Maya’s investigation, and the solution.

questions.text: What lesson is best supported by Maya’s actions?
options: Festivals should never be held during the rainy season
questions.feedback: Maya asks questions, uses evidence, and learns the reason before making assumptions.

missions.title: The Chronicles of Wisdom
missions.story: At the village learning fair, two friends see the same event differently. Learners explore different points of view, text purposes, and clear writing.
missions.focus: Point of view and character comparison; author’s purpose and types of texts; paragraph organization, grammar and writing.

finalChallenge.title: Publish the Community Page
finalChallenge.description: Publish the Community Page: place three sentence cards in order, identify one sentence with correct grammar, then compose a 2–3 sentence report about a classroom activity (record text for teacher review).

steps.prompt: Publish the Community Page: tap the three sentences in the correct order.
items: First, our class planned a reading hour.
Next, learners shared their favorite books.
Finally, everyone promised to read at home.

steps.prompt: Which sentence has correct grammar?
items: The learners shares their books.
The learners share their books.
The learner share their books.
The learners is sharing their books.

steps.prompt: Write a short report (2 to 3 sentences) about a classroom activity. Your teacher will read it.

checkpoints.title: Mirror Hall — Two Perspectives
checkpoints.reading: Anna and Ben attended the Brightville Festival. Anna said, “I loved watching the colorful parade. Music and dancing make me happy.” Ben said, “I enjoyed the history museum because I learned about our heroes.” Both attended the same festival, but each preferred a different activity.
checkpoints.lesson: The first-person point of view uses words such as “I” and “we.” Compare characters by identifying similarities and differences, then infer what their words reveal.

miniGame.name: Perspective Match
miniGame.instructions: Drag each statement to Anna, Ben, or Both. Example: “Enjoys the parade” → Anna; “Attended the festival” → Both.

steps.prompt: Perspective Match: who does each statement describe?
items: Enjoys the parade
Likes music and dancing
Learned about heroes at the museum
Enjoyed the history museum
Attended the Brightville Festival
steps.success: You compared the two points of view correctly.

questions.text: Which pronoun in Anna’s words shows first-person point of view?
questions.feedback: The word “I” identifies the speaker’s own point of view.

questions.text: Which activity did Anna enjoy most?
questions.feedback: Anna says she loved watching the parade.

questions.text: Why did Ben enjoy the museum?
questions.feedback: Ben values the history facts he learned there.

questions.text: What do Anna and Ben have in common?
questions.feedback: They share the festival experience although their interests differ.

questions.text: Which sentence best summarizes the passage?
options: Two friends attended the same festival but preferred different activities
questions.feedback: This sentence captures the common event and different preferences.

checkpoints.title: Book Maze — Find the Purpose
checkpoints.reading: Book A: “A puppy followed its owner through the busy market, but soon it lost its way. A kind vendor helped it return home.” Book B: “Rivers carry water from higher land to lower areas and may flow into lakes or seas.” Book C: “Help keep Brightville River clean! Put litter in bins and join our Saturday clean-up.”
checkpoints.lesson: A narrative tells events; an informational text explains facts; a persuasive text encourages a decision or action. The author’s purpose guides word choice and organization.

miniGame.name: Three-Book Sorting
miniGame.instructions: Sort the three book cards into Narrative, Informational and Persuasive; identify evidence words before submitting.

steps.prompt: Three-Book Sorting: what kind of text is each book?
items: Book A: A puppy followed its owner through the busy market, but soon it lost its way. A kind vendor helped it return home.
Book B: Rivers carry water from higher land to lower areas and may flow into lakes or seas.
Book C: Help keep Brightville River clean! Put litter in bins and join our Saturday clean-up.
steps.success: You matched each book to the author's purpose.

steps.prompt: Which words from Book C show that it is persuasive?
items: Put litter in bins and join our Saturday clean-up.
Rivers carry water from higher land to lower areas.
A kind vendor helped it return home.
Soon it lost its way.

questions.text: What type of text is Book A about the lost puppy?
questions.feedback: Book A tells a sequence of story events.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of Book B about rivers?
questions.feedback: Book B explains how rivers flow.

questions.text: What does Book C want readers to do?
questions.feedback: It uses a call to action to encourage river protection.

questions.text: Which phrase is a clear call to action?
questions.feedback: This phrase directly asks people to participate.

questions.text: Which pairing is correct?
questions.feedback: Book B gives facts and Book C encourages action.

checkpoints.title: Writer’s Workshop — Community Report
checkpoints.reading: Our class held a Community Day. First, we cleaned the school garden. Next, we planted flowers beside the walkway. Finally, our teacher thanked everyone for helping. The class felt proud of its work.
checkpoints.lesson: A clear paragraph has a main idea and supporting details in logical order. Correct subject–verb agreement and punctuation help readers understand the message.

miniGame.name: Paragraph Builder
miniGame.instructions: Arrange three sentence cards into beginning, middle and ending. Then choose correct grammar forms and write two sentences about a school activity.

steps.prompt: Paragraph Builder: tap the sentences in the order of beginning, middle and ending.
items: First, we cleaned the school garden.
Next, we planted flowers beside the walkway.
Finally, our teacher thanked everyone for helping.

steps.prompt: Which sentence uses the correct verb?
items: The students plants flowers.
The students plant flowers.
The student plant flowers.
The students is planting flowers.

steps.prompt: Write two sentences about a school activity.

questions.text: Which sentence is a clear topic sentence for the paragraph?
options: Our class held a Community Day.
questions.feedback: It introduces the main event described by the paragraph.

questions.text: Which happened immediately after the garden was cleaned?
options: The class went to the market
questions.feedback: The paragraph uses “Next” before planting flowers.

questions.text: Which sentence uses correct subject–verb agreement?
questions.feedback: Plural “students” agrees with “plant.”

questions.text: Which sentence is complete?
questions.feedback: This choice has a subject and a complete predicate.

questions.text: Which sentence gives the best ending for the paragraph?
options: Everyone felt proud of helping the school.
questions.feedback: The closing sentence summarizes the group’s positive experience.

missions.title: The Explorer’s Atlas
missions.story: The village museum needs a reliable information exhibit. Learners check sources, organize notes, and interpret posters before completing the Explorer’s Atlas.
missions.focus: Information literacy, main idea and evidence; sequencing and simple reports; visual/multimedia messages and audience.

finalChallenge.title: Complete the Explorer’s Atlas
finalChallenge.description: Complete the Explorer’s Atlas: choose two trustworthy facts for an exhibit, arrange Lina’s observations chronologically, and build a simple school-cleanliness poster with a heading and relevant image.

steps.prompt: Complete the Explorer's Atlas: choose TWO trustworthy facts for the exhibit.
items: The Philippine Eagle is found only in the Philippines.
The Philippine Eagle lives only in deserts.
The Philippine Eagle is critically endangered.
The Philippine Eagle eats only fish.

steps.prompt: Arrange Lina's observations in the order they happened.
items: Our group hiked to Eagle Hill.
We watched birds and wrote notes about their behavior.
We returned to camp.
We shared our observations with the class.

steps.prompt: Build the school-cleanliness poster. Choose the heading.
items: KEEP OUR SCHOOL CLEAN!
Maybe clean, maybe not
Eagles are big
Go home early

steps.prompt: Now choose the relevant image.
items: Children putting waste in the correct bins
A mountain at night
A birthday cake
A broken chair

checkpoints.title: Grand Library — Reliable Sources
checkpoints.reading: Source A (encyclopedia): The Philippine Eagle is a very large bird of prey found only in the Philippines. It is critically endangered. Source B (science reference): The Philippine Eagle lives in Philippine forests and hunts a variety of animals. Source C (anonymous note): “The Philippine Eagle lives only in deserts and eats only fish.”
checkpoints.lesson: Reliable sources help support statements with evidence. Compare texts for consistent facts, find the main idea, and identify claims that do not match the evidence.

miniGame.name: Source Sorting
miniGame.instructions: Sort statement cards into “Supported by Sources A/B” and “Not supported.” Tap a source label to inspect the text.

steps.prompt: Source Sorting: is each statement supported by Sources A and B?
steps.context:
Source A (encyclopedia): The Philippine Eagle is a very large bird of prey found only in the Philippines. It is critically endangered.
Source B (science reference): The Philippine Eagle lives in Philippine forests and hunts a variety of animals.
Source C (anonymous note): “The Philippine Eagle lives only in deserts and eats only fish.”
items: The Philippine Eagle is found only in the Philippines.
The Philippine Eagle is critically endangered.
The Philippine Eagle lives in forests.
The Philippine Eagle lives only in deserts.
The Philippine Eagle eats only fish.
buckets: Supported by Sources A and B
steps.success: Reliable sources agree with each other. Well sorted!

questions.text: What is the shared topic of Sources A and B?
questions.feedback: Both references describe the Philippine Eagle.

questions.text: Which statement is supported by Source A?
options: It is found only in the Philippines
It is a type of fish
questions.feedback: Source A directly states the bird is found in the Philippines.

questions.text: Which statement is NOT supported by Sources A and B?
options: It is a bird of prey
questions.feedback: The references describe forest habitats, not deserts only.

questions.text: Which source should be checked most carefully before being trusted?
questions.feedback: An unsupported anonymous statement needs verification.

questions.text: Which is the best summary of Sources A and B?
options: The Philippine Eagle is a large endangered bird living in Philippine forests
The bird is found only in deserts
questions.feedback: This combines the key facts without adding unsupported information.

checkpoints.title: Messenger’s Camp — Organize the Report
checkpoints.reading: Explorer Lina’s log: “First, our group hiked to Eagle Hill. Next, we watched birds and wrote notes about their behavior. Afterward, we returned to camp. Finally, we shared our observations with the class.”
checkpoints.lesson: A short report organizes factual events in a logical sequence. Use first, next, afterward and finally to guide readers; include observations rather than unrelated opinions.

miniGame.name: Report Organizer
miniGame.instructions: Arrange four event cards in order. Choose the best report heading and complete a two-sentence observation report.

steps.prompt: Report Organizer: tap the four events in order.
items: Our group hiked to Eagle Hill.
We watched birds and wrote notes about their behavior.
We returned to camp.
We shared our observations with the class.

steps.prompt: Which is the best heading for the report?
items: Observation Report: Birds at Eagle Hill
My Favorite Day Ever
Why Everyone Must Visit Eagle Hill
A Scary Hike

steps.prompt: Write a two-sentence observation report about the bird watching.

questions.text: What did the group do first?
questions.feedback: The log begins with the hike to Eagle Hill.

questions.text: What happened immediately after the hike?
options: They observed birds and took notes
questions.feedback: The word “Next” introduces the bird observations.

questions.text: Which title best fits Lina’s report?
questions.feedback: The report is about observing and recording birds at Eagle Hill.

questions.text: Which sentence reports a specific observation?
options: Birds are the best animals ever.
We observed birds gathering near the trees.
questions.feedback: The last sentence describes something the group could observe.

questions.text: Which is the best final step in preparing the report?
options: Arrange findings clearly and share them
questions.feedback: Organized findings make the report useful to readers.

checkpoints.title: Gallery of Messages — Read the Poster
checkpoints.reading: School poster: “KEEP OUR SCHOOL CLEAN! Put waste in the correct bins. Bring reusable containers. Join the Friday Clean-Up Drive.” The poster shows a green recycling symbol, a bin, and children helping each other.
checkpoints.lesson: A visual message uses words, symbols and layout to communicate with an audience. Identify its purpose, intended audience and the evidence in the image and text.

miniGame.name: Poster Builder
miniGame.instructions: Match poster symbols with meanings, then select a clear message and a relevant picture for a new school poster.

steps.prompt: Poster Builder: what does each poster symbol mean?
items: Green recycling symbol
A bin
Children helping each other
buckets: Throw waste in the right place
steps.success: You read the poster's symbols correctly.

steps.prompt: Choose the clearest message for a new school poster.
items: Keep our school clean: use the bins!
Clean is maybe good.
Poster poster poster.
Do whatever you want with waste.

steps.prompt: Choose the picture that fits the message best.
items: Children putting litter in a bin
A cat sleeping on a sofa
A race car on a track
A pile of litter on the floor

questions.text: What is the main purpose of the poster?
questions.feedback: The poster asks the school community to keep the school clean.

questions.text: Who is the poster mainly intended for?
questions.feedback: The message addresses people in the school.

questions.text: Which image best supports the poster?
options: A student sorting litter into bins
questions.feedback: The image directly reinforces the clean-up message.

questions.text: Which line is a call to action?
questions.feedback: This sentence asks readers to take part in an activity.

questions.text: Which combination best communicates the message?
options: Clear short words with relevant recycling images
questions.feedback: Short readable text and related symbols reinforce each other.
